Decisions Already Made
Ayoub Merimi and Souhail Bakkali and Abdeljalil Sakat
Abstract
Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the mo-
ment it is made; the action it commits to is la-
tent, carried out later, in a changing world. We
therefore introduce a timestamp theory of deci-
sion validity and a decision ledger that realises
it. Six timestamps define a decision; a fresh-
ness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence
guarantees at action time, placing the remain-
ing risk in information published afterwards.
Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities:
routing, which delivers that information to af-
fected decisions before their revision deadlines,
and temporal judgment, which reads it for the
time of action. The ledger is persistent state
holding each decision’s times, evidence and
background knowledge, indexed by watch con-
ditions written at decision time. Controlled
decision streams with exact labels confirm four
predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to fron-
tier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the
accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on de-
cisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows
routing; the ledger’s index sets what routing
reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect
dependencies at low exposure; and the remain-
ing errors concern when a change takes effect.
Freshness makes a decision right when it is
made; routing and temporal judgment keep it
right when it is carried out.
1 Introduction

in the Bellhaven district. At 18:40, the grid op-

plies without power; the Gorran substation supplies
the Bellhaven district (Figure 1). The choice was
right at 13:05 and is wrong at 20:30. The informa-
tion that settles it appeared after the decision and
refers to the restaurant only through the substation

8 Conclusion
Freshness is necessary for LLM decision-making
and insufficient on its own. A decision is judged
when it is carried out, the freshness ceiling bounds
7

what evidence at decision time can guarantee, and
the accuracy that remains is set by routing and
judgment (Eq. 3). The controlled tests confirm
each prediction: freshness alone leaves changing
decisions stale, delivery is sufficient for change and
recall follows what the ledger indexes, misleading
deliveries cost correct decisions in proportion to
weak judgment, and the residual error is mostly
temporal. The theory yields three design princi-
ples for LLM agents:recordeach decision with
its times and what it depends on;routenews to it
until its revision deadline, through an index written
when the decision is made; andrevalidateit by
checking when each change is in effect.
Limitations
Controlled streams.The decision streams are
synthetic by design: exact control over timing, ref-
erence and labels is what lets each prediction be
tested in isolation. Real news is longer and nois-
ier, dependencies can be implicit, and relevance
can be uncertain, so the magnitudes we report be-
long to these streams while the predictions concern
mechanisms. Testing the theory on logged agent
decisions, and in languages beyond English, is the
next step.
Scope of the theory.The theory models a deci-
sion as a choice among options with one revision
deadline and a binary outcome, and the freshness
ceiling assumes a constant hazard rate. Real com-
mitments are staged, partly reversible and graded
in utility, and facts change in bursts. The factori-
sation of Eq. 3 carries over, because information
must reach a decision before it can change it, but
its terms then depend on time and on the cost of
revising.
Reach of the ledger.Routing recall is bounded
by the dependencies the ledger records at decision
time, and the ledger treats routed news as trustwor-
thy. Discovering dependencies after the decision
and weighing the credibility of sources extend the
ledger beyond this paper.
Ethics Statement
The decision streams use fictional entities and con-
tain no personal data, and hosted models were
queried on this synthetic data only. Systems that
revise decisions on a user’s behalf can act on false
or adversarial news; routing should be paired with
source verification and, for consequential decisions,
with user confirmation.
